title: ‘It’s the End of the World as We Know It’: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Changing Landscape of Legal Practice and Education
author: Lachlan Robb · Rachel Hews · Felicity Deane · Michael Guihot · Jonah Farry · Amanda Kennedy

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The supplied excerpts focus on GenAI’s effects on legal practice, professional ethics and Australian legal education. They do not provide findings or arguments about cheaper consumer legal assistance, access to justice, UPL boundaries, self-representation outcomes or provider reform, so the source’s position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.
qs: Drawing on empirical research, we present findings from interviews with 51 participants across 27 organisations in which we aim to evaluate what it means to practise law alongside GenAI.6 In the analysis of the interview data, we consider the impact of GenAI upon the profession and whether these impacts will challenge long-held traditions associated with the ethical practice of law.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s concern that GenAI affects professional ethics and lawyer preparation, and it introduces an empirical study of those issues. However, the supplied excerpt contains only the study’s rationale and scope, not findings or recommendations showing whether the authors endorse active scrutiny under existing duties or a particular governance approach.
qs: GenAI has drawn significant attention for its capacity to undertake tasks traditionally carried out by lawyers, many of which are now being completed, at least in part, by machines.3 These developments have prompted important questions not only for the profession, but also for the universities and law schools responsible for preparing our future lawyers.

Drawing on empirical research, we present findings from interviews with 51 participants across 27 organisations in which we aim to evaluate what it means to practise law alongside GenAI.6 In the analysis of the interview data, we consider the impact of GenAI upon the profession and whether these impacts will challenge long-held traditions associated with the ethical practice of law.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central proposition that foundational legal judgment and GenAI competence must be developed together. It materially extends that position by proposing early, integrated technological and ethical foundations, critical verification skills, and sustained shared training pathways between law schools and the profession, while treating weakened junior-learning pathways as a prospective rather than established harm.
qs: While doctrinal training remains essential, graduates must also be equipped to critically evaluate GenAI- generated outputs, understand the limitations and risks of automated systems, and navigate new ethical, financial, and professional challenges.

An important way to support this shift is through sustained, structured collaboration between law schools and key stakeholders across the legal ecosystem, including law firms, community legal centres, in-house legal teams, government legal departments, regulatory bodies, and legal technology providers.

st.an: The source accepts the need to preserve legal expertise for meaningful oversight and materially develops the cluster’s educational implications. It advocates combining adaptable, technology-neutral AI literacy with legal knowledge, ethics, critical thinking and interpersonal skills rather than treating prompting as sufficient competence. Its support rests on practitioner interviews and argument, not measured educational outcomes.

st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central distinction between AI exposure and professional readiness: foundational legal expertise and human verification remain indispensable. It materially develops that proposition through a staged curriculum—baseline literacy, controlled mid-degree use and responsible later use—and shared university–profession responsibility for replacing training opportunities that automation may erode.

Mid-degree subjects can deepen foundational knowledge and may include an option to allow the use of GenAI in controlled circumstances.194 These mid-degree uses will allow students to reflect on their GenAI usage which in turn will teach students about the hallucination risks, biases, and limitations.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s augmentation-over-replacement framing and verification boundary, then materially develops its central competence-risk proposition through qualitative Australian evidence on the “5-year problem.” It further proposes a concrete response: shared, structured collaboration among legal educators, employers, regulators and other stakeholders to rebuild training pathways as junior work is automated.
qs: Participants in the study commented on a ‘5-year problem’, where it is unclear how junior lawyers will obtain necessary fundamental skills, particularly if GenAI reduces the demand for law graduates and alters traditional training pathways by assuming responsibility for mundane, yet essential tasks.

An important way to support this shift is through sustained, structured collaboration between law schools and key stakeholders across the legal ecosystem, including law firms, community legal centres, in-house legal teams, government legal departments, regulatory bodies, and legal technology providers.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s supervised-aid model: GenAI should enhance rather than replace legal capability, and skilled lawyers must interrogate its outputs. It materially develops the cluster by grounding concerns about verification capacity and junior deskilling in interviews across Australian legal organisations and proposing a degree-wide redesign of legal education to preserve doctrinal competence while teaching critical and ethical AI use.
qs: The role of the GenAI-enhanced lawyer is one of symbiosis with the technology; if a lawyer lacks skills, they cannot use the technology to fill these gaps.

While doctrinal training remains essential, graduates must also be equipped to critically evaluate GenAI- generated outputs, understand the limitations and risks of automated systems, and navigate new ethical, financial, and professional challenges.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source strongly accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, human-led augmentation: current gains are task-specific, lawyer replacement is not imminent, and verification remains essential. It materially extends that account by linking automation of junior work to the future reviewer pipeline and proposing technology-neutral legal education grounded in legal knowledge, ethics, verification and human skills.
qs: Overall, the interview results illustrate that AI is (already) actively reshaping legal work, roles, and required skills, but it does not appear to be replacing lawyers entirely.

As stated in the above results, the ‘5-year problem’ reveals the tension that the legal profession needs to continue to hire graduates despite GenAI’s ability to undertake tasks traditionally performed by graduates.

st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s cautious account: it describes generative AI as probabilistic language generation used chiefly for legal text, while emphasizing that legal language, discretion and interpretive openness remain difficult to automate. It also treats labour transformation as prospective and raises ethical concerns about unchecked adoption, though it does not itself develop the cluster’s specific verification and governance requirements.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk

kp.k: Australian interviews document adoption, not settled workforce outcomes
kp.d: The authors conducted semi-structured interviews with 51 participants from 27 organisations between August and November 2024, using purposive and snowball sampling. Most participants were based in Brisbane, Melbourne, or Sydney. The sample included law firms, community legal centres, an in-house team, government, judiciary, professional services and technology providers; roles included 20 partners, eight lawyers, five junior lawyers, seven technology specialists, one commissioner and 10 senior organisational representatives. Transcripts were manually corrected and analysed inductively using NVivo. These findings describe reported experiences and expectations rather than a measured profession-wide employment effect.
qs: Between August and November 2024, we conducted interviews with 51 participants from 27 unique organisations.
Participants were recruited using a combination of purposive and snowball sampling.

kp.k: Participants expect augmentation rather than lawyers’ wholesale replacement
kp.d: The authors report that participants generally interpreted GenAI as changing legal work rather than ending the profession. Partners often anticipated more engaging graduate work, whereas juniors feared more competitive entry and questioned whether they would be hired today. Most participants regarded future outcomes as uncertain; some considered dramatic displacement predictions too speculative to guide firm strategy. The authors also reject treating the profession as powerless to shape adoption.
qs: The broad message from the interviewees was that this is not the end of the profession, but there are critical changes that are happening as a result of the introduction of this technology.
Ultimately the majority of those interviewed expressed uncertainty, suggesting that the future is unknowable.

kp.k: Hiring effects vary across firm sizes and timeframes
kp.d: During the interviews, larger national firms generally anticipated few immediate hiring changes, while smaller firms viewed AI as a force multiplier that could reduce recruitment needs. Graduate programmes were mainly changing recruitment criteria rather than numbers. A subsequent April 2025 email from one participant reported avoiding at least one hire after integrating AI into daily practice. This follow-up is an individual reported outcome, distinct from the predominantly speculative hiring expectations recorded in 2024.
qs: At the time of the research, this change was speculative and very few hiring practices were being changed.
The core change was seen in graduate programs that were making slight changes to hiring criteria, but not to numbers.
I’ve avoided hiring at least one new person in my new firm as we have unlocked so much efficiency on basic tasks

kp.k: The five-year problem threatens the experienced-lawyer pipeline
kp.d: Participants frequently compared GenAI output with a clerk’s or first-rotation graduate’s first draft: potentially useful but requiring senior verification. The authors identify a prospective ‘5-year problem’: replacing junior tasks or reducing graduate recruitment could deprive future lawyers of the experience necessary to become competent associates and partners. Participants warned that short-term recruitment savings could create later skills shortages; this is a pipeline concern, not evidence that such shortages had already occurred.
qs: the profession then faces what this research dubs the ‘5-year problem’ relating to the loss of experience within the first five years of a lawyer’s work.
It’s like having a first rotation grad.
It’s a starting point.

kp.k: Six task categories reveal uneven adoption and risk
kp.d: The interviews identified personal productivity, condensing, checking, learning, drafting and predicting. Administrative productivity was a common, comparatively low-risk entry point; condensing covered summaries and simplification, checking covered document inconsistencies and proofreading, and learning covered research and orientation to unfamiliar law. Research and drafting were regarded as riskier and dependent on lawyer review. Prediction was not broadly discussed and, the authors clarify, does not specifically rely on GenAI. Grace, an international-firm partner, reported one to two hours of weekly personal-productivity savings; this was an interview claim rather than a controlled measurement.
qs: These were: personal productivity, condensing, checking, learning, drafting, and predicting.
‘[W]e’re seeing time savings of between one and two hours a week from lawyers using [Office 365] for a wide range of personal productivity tasks’.
Prediction uses are law-adjacent and do not specifically use GenAI.

kp.k: Verification and data governance constrain substantive legal uses
kp.d: Participants associated legal research with hallucination risk and stressed verification before reliance. Firms were reluctant to discuss fully generated first drafts, instead emphasising checking and lower-risk administrative uses. Security concerns extended beyond where client data is stored to where it is processed and where the model operates. The prevailing model was lawyer-supervised augmentation, not direct reliance on unreviewed client-facing output.
qs: Participants were consistent in identifying this as a riskier use for GenAI because of the risk of hallucinations and the need to verify any information returned by the system.
Firms were reluctant to openly discuss the extent to which drafting and generation was being used to entirely create first drafts.
Where’s it stored? But also where’s it processed?

kp.k: Community legal assistance brings benefits and litigation risks
kp.d: Community legal services reported slow adoption but described free tools helping clients with limited literacy begin simple letters. This was distinguished from using GenAI for legal advice or court submissions. The article also reports fabricated citations by self-represented litigants and discusses Queensland Courts guidance for non-lawyers dated 15 September 2025. A judicial participant warned that easier generation of lengthy submissions and numerous case references could slow adjudication rather than streamline it. The literature review separately presents improved access and second-class justice as competing possibilities, not established outcomes.
qs: For community legal services, GenAI has been adopted slowly, but even free- use tools can be useful to allow clients to help themselves.
I don’t use it for submissions.
I think it’s got the potential to actually make decision making slower from the jurisdiction

kp.k: Outcome prediction raises participation and regulatory concerns
kp.d: A judicial interviewee envisaged tools summarising a commissioner’s previous decisions, potentially helping parties recognise weak appeals, but worried about discouraging legitimate claims. The authors discuss TheoAi and Canotera as commercial examples, attributing prediction capabilities to company claims rather than independently established performance. They contrast this with France’s prohibition under article 33 of its Justice Reform Act on specified uses of magistrate and court registry member identities for evaluative or predictive purposes.
qs: But then I’d hate for people to be discouraged from running their matter because they think that they know what the answer is going to be.
clear predictions about your case’s likely outcomes, potential damages, and timelines

kp.k: Hourly billing creates an adoption and pricing tension
kp.d: The authors explain that Australian state-based costs regulation requires fair and reasonable charges and argue that firms cannot bill lawyer time that was not actually worked. This could deter GenAI adoption under hourly billing, even where it improves efficiency. Participants differed: some expected little billing disruption, while others saw lower internal costs, cheaper matters and greater throughput as competitive advantages. The article treats future resolution through professional bodies, legislation and courts as uncertain.
qs: This is because a legal practice cannot charge for time not actually undertaken by a lawyer.
The inability to bill for work may be one barrier to the adoption of GenAI in the legal profession.
We want to bill our clients less for these matters, because we become more competitive.

kp.k: Alternative charges redistribute AI costs and review intensity
kp.d: Interviewees described or proposed higher hourly rates to recover technology costs, specific AI charges and tiered services priced according to human review. One participant reported a firm offering AI-only due diligence, light-touch lawyer review and fuller human review at different price and risk levels. These are reported practices and proposals, not findings that such models comply with applicable billing duties. The authors warn against competition reducing service quality.
qs: An interesting alternative has been the proposal of a tiered system where clients are able to opt into different models of charging depending on how much GenAI is used.
you can choose a model where you do an AI only due diligence and that has a certain price
What is certain is that the profession will need to avoid an inevitable race to the bottom in terms of quality of service.

kp.k: Human judgement and legal knowledge remain essential
kp.d: Interviewees prioritised empathy, trust, communication, legal reasoning and critical thinking alongside technological literacy. Graduates need enough substantive knowledge to identify errors, understand tool limitations and frame the right questions. The authors argue that AI cannot compensate for missing foundational legal competence, because competent human verification depends on that knowledge. Some firms expected to teach tool use internally while recruiting for the ability to critique outputs.
qs: The core required skill becomes one of verifying and interrogating the outputs of the technology:
I think the ability to critique and evaluate the output is going to be even more important.
if a lawyer lacks skills, they cannot use the technology to fill these gaps.

kp.k: Technology-neutral literacy takes priority over transient prompting techniques
kp.d: Participants wanted graduates to understand AI capabilities, data sources, risks and appropriate interaction, without generally requiring them to build or code systems. Although prompting was frequently valued, the authors caution that interfaces and automated prompt improvement could change its importance, making an undergraduate commitment to specialised prompting premature. Their recommendation is broader competence combining legal knowledge, professional ethics and technological understanding; coding and advanced prompting may remain suitable electives.
qs: I think the most important thing is to teach [AI] in almost a tech neutral approach, because the technology will change so quickly
Hence, although prompting was identified as an important skill at the time of writing, its inclusion in an undergraduate degree may be premature due to the expected evolution of the technology.
it is not a simple matter of ‘prompting skills’

kp.k: The mundane-work paradox demands intentional training
kp.d: Participants credited repetitive early-career work with developing expertise while also identifying it as a prime automation target. The authors propose retaining such tasks deliberately for learning rather than repeating them solely to deliver work. A partner suggested diminishing educational returns well before reviewing 1,000 documents; the article’s suggestion that 20 might suffice is a possibility, not a validated training threshold. Faster learning and better retention are potential benefits, conditional on firms preserving meaningful junior experience instead of eliminating the graduate stage.
qs: One problem that was identified by the use of GenAI in firms is the ‘mundane work paradox’.
However, whereas in the past doing the same task 1,000 times was needed, 20 may be enough to provide the learning opportunity.
Ultimately, there was no clear solution to this problem presented by the interview participants, other than to suggest it was a problem that would be shared with universities.

kp.k: Curriculum reform should stage AI use around foundational competence
kp.d: The authors recommend introductory instruction on AI capabilities, ethical boundaries, academic misconduct and risks to knowledge development; controlled mid-degree use to examine hallucinations, bias and limitations; and responsible research and enhancement uses in final year. Advanced technical electives could support interested students. They argue that doctrinal knowledge remains essential and that premature reliance on AI is risky when students cannot yet judge its accuracy. They also acknowledge resource constraints and uneven technology adoption across future employers.
qs: introductory law subjects must create a baseline understanding of the technology.
The ethical use of GenAI should be emphasised throughout any law degree.
These mid-degree uses will allow students to reflect on their GenAI usage which in turn will teach students about the hallucination risks, biases, and limitations.

kp.k: Professional formation requires shared institutional responsibility
kp.d: Suggested responses include stronger mentoring, apprenticeships, practical legal training, clinical education and extended placements. Drawing on interviews and Australian education-policy reports, the authors recommend formal collaboration among universities, firms, community legal centres, in-house teams, government, professional bodies, regulators and technology providers. Proposed mechanisms include co-designed curricula, shared training and assessments simulating AI-assisted practice, with attention to admission requirements. They report little structured university collaboration despite changes to firms’ internal training and identify this as an area for further research.
qs: law firms are already changing their internal training models, but there is little structured collaboration with universities to prepare graduates for these shifts.
Responding to GenAI in the legal profession requires more than adding a technology subject to the curriculum.
This is an area that warrants further research and attention within both academic and policy contexts.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors describe ongoing augmentation of legal work rather than wholesale replacement of lawyers, alongside possible reductions in junior recruitment, disruption of training pathways, billing changes, and new educational requirements.
pts.d: Robb and colleagues report that GenAI is already changing workflows through personal productivity, condensing information, checking documents, research or learning, and drafting. They also discuss prediction tools, expressly distinguishing these from specifically generative AI. Interviewees generally anticipate more efficient lawyers rather than the disappearance of the profession. Grace, an international-firm partner, reports personal-productivity savings of one to two hours weekly; Dominic, a small-firm lawyer, estimates at least a 30% reduction in time for certain document reviews. Smaller practices may use AI to expand services or avoid hiring, while larger national firms generally anticipated few immediate recruitment changes. The authors identify a '5-year problem': automating junior tasks could remove the practical experience needed to produce future skilled lawyers. Their 'mundane work paradox' is that repetitive tasks are both candidates for automation and perceived sources of expertise. They suggest deliberately retaining learning opportunities could allow faster development and potentially improve retention, rather than eliminating the graduate stage. Interviewees describe competing billing responses: lower fees and greater throughput, increased hourly rates to recover technology costs, separate AI charges, and tiers differentiated by human review. These are alternatives, not a settled market outcome. Community legal interviewees describe assistance with clients' writing, while Katherine, a judicial commissioner, warns that AI-enabled proliferation of submissions and authorities could slow adjudication. The authors argue that graduates need legal knowledge, human communication skills, ethical reasoning, and the ability to verify AI output; universities and the profession should jointly redesign education and practical training.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The primary evidence is qualitative interview testimony, supplemented by an April 2025 hiring update, published reports, legal authorities, and literature; most future outcomes are interviewee expectations or author proposals rather than measured effects.
pts.d: The study uses semi-structured interviews with 51 participants from 27 Australian organisations, recruited through purposive and snowball sampling beginning with the researchers' professional networks. Participants included partners, lawyers, juniors, technology specialists, a commissioner, and senior organisational representatives. Interviews were transcribed, manually checked, and analysed inductively using NVivo; quotations from 34 participants appear in the article. Reported productivity savings are attributed to individual interviewees, not presented as controlled performance measurements or representative sector averages. During quotation confirmation in April 2025, Caleb reported avoiding at least one hire after integrating AI into daily practice; this is a subsequent individual account, distinct from the original interview period. The training-gap mechanism rests principally on participants' accounts of learning through practice and anticipated automation, supported by legal-education literature and Queensland Law Society reports. Proposed benefits from fewer repetitions, faster progression, or improved retention are not demonstrated by an intervention study. Billing analysis combines interview proposals with Australian state-based fair-and-reasonable-cost requirements. Discussion of self-represented litigants includes Katherine's observations, a published fake-case incident, and Queensland Courts guidance; these are not measured hallucination rates. The literature review's forecasts of professional extinction or replacement of adjudication are contextual arguments, not empirical findings of this study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The central observational window is August–November 2024, with some 2025 updates; longer-term recruitment and training effects remain conditional and uncertain.
pts.d: The authors distinguish adoption already occurring during the interviews from expected future changes. Few hiring practices had changed at that stage, although the April 2025 follow-up supplies one account of an avoided hire. The '5-year problem' concerns experience normally acquired during the first five years of practice, rather than a precise forecast that a quantified shortage will occur five years after publication. Its severity depends on whether firms replace entry-level work or preserve deliberate training and graduate recruitment. The authors' dominant model is human-in-the-loop augmentation: research and drafting require knowledgeable lawyers to check outputs before reliance. More sensitive uses face hallucination, confidentiality, offshore storage, and processing concerns. Billing effects depend on applicable charging rules, technology costs, client demand, and the extent of human review; the article does not establish which model will prevail. Skills recommendations are qualified by changing interfaces: prompting was considered useful during the study, but the authors caution against overcommitting curricula to potentially short-lived techniques. They propose baseline AI and ethical awareness early in the degree, controlled uses in middle years, and more advanced use or electives later. They also stress that practice adoption varies, so some graduates will initially rely more heavily on traditional skills.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Effects differ across juniors, established practitioners, firm sizes, clients, courts, and education providers; the source does not claim a uniform market-wide outcome.
pts.d: Graduates, clerks, and paralegals face possible substitution of routine tasks and a loss of apprenticeship opportunities, but also prospects of earlier client contact and more engaging work. Some juniors anticipate tougher entry competition, whereas many partners emphasise the benefits of removing menial work. Established lawyers gain potential productivity but retain responsibility for verification and need to adapt. Smaller firms may expand their capabilities without additional staff; larger firms anticipate augmentation of complex matters with less immediate change to graduate intake. Clients may receive cheaper services or choose different levels of human review, but quality and ethical charging remain concerns. Community legal centre clients with limited literacy can receive drafting assistance; self-represented litigants risk reliance on fabricated authorities, and courts may face greater volumes of material. Prediction systems could discourage weak claims but might also deter litigants from pursuing matters. Universities, practical legal training providers, law firms, regulators, and professional bodies are assigned shared responsibility for preserving foundational competence while developing AI literacy. The authors advocate structured partnerships rather than treating education reform as solely the universities' obligation.
